title: Ambareesha Charitram
body:
Ambareesha Charitram

In the illustrious line of the Ikshvaku dynasty there was born a king named Ambareesha, whose heart belonged entirely to Sriman Narayana. Though he ruled with wisdom, justice, and great strength, his true wealth lay in his devotion. To him nothing belonged to himself, for everything belonged to the Lord; his rule was marked by charity and compassion, and he saw no distinction between himself and the humblest of his subjects. So complete was his surrender that the Lord's own Sudarshana Chakra had, as it were, taken it upon itself to rush to Ambareesha's protection whenever he had need.
Ambareesha observed the Dwadashi-Vratam with unwavering discipline. Having fasted through Ekadashi, one must break the fast within a certain span of time at the start of Dwadashi, and feed one's guests before eating. On one such occasion, just as the king prepared to break his fast, the great sage Durvasa Maharishi arrived at his court. Received with full honors, Durvasa said he would first bathe in the river and then return to share the meal, and the king, bound by the duty of hospitality, agreed to wait.
But hours passed, and Durvasa did not return. The auspicious window for breaking the fast was slipping away, and Ambareesha found himself caught between two duties — if he ate before his guest he would dishonor his hospitality, yet if he delayed further his vrata would be broken. On the counsel of the sage Vasishta, he chose the path that satisfied both: he took a sip of holy water, which technically did not break the fast yet fulfilled the vrata's requirement. At that very moment Durvasa returned, and, sensing what had happened, erupted in fury, accusing the king of dishonoring a guest through arrogance. Ambareesha stood silent, hands folded, having meant no disrespect — but to a mind consumed by anger even an innocent act appears as an offense.
From the depths of his yogic power Durvasa tore a lock of his matted hair and hurled it to the ground, and from it arose a monstrous, blazing demon that charged toward the king to devour him. The court fell into chaos, but Ambareesha stood unmoved, his mind resting upon the Lord. Before the demon could reach him, the Sudarshana Chakra blazed through the sky and reduced the fearsome being to ash in an instant. And then the discus turned upon Durvasa himself.
The sage fled. He ran across the earth, but Sudarshana followed. He ascended to the heavens seeking refuge among the Devas, but even Indra dared not interfere. He rushed to Brahma, but the creator bowed in helplessness; he went to Kailasa, but Shiva told him plainly that no one can stay the Lord's justice once it is set in motion, and sent him to the only one who could save him — Sriman Narayana Himself. Falling at the Lord's feet in Vaikuntham, Durvasa begged for mercy, but the Lord answered that His Sudarshana moves only for His devotees and cannot be recalled at His command; the only one who could save the sage was Ambareesha, the very man he had wronged.
With no other path left, Durvasa returned to Ambareesha, his pride shattered, and fell at the king's feet pleading forgiveness. But Ambareesha, purest of devotees, had never held any anger in his heart; his only concern throughout had been for the sage's well-being. With a simple prayer he asked that the sage be spared, and the Sudarshana halted, its fire dimming, the sky growing calm once more. Durvasa departed humbled, and Ambareesha simply continued his vrata — untroubled, knowing that one who surrenders completely to the Lord is always protected.
